title: Flash Sale Checkout
summary: A midnight sale drives 3,200 orders per second into a database that can commit 1,000. More read replicas won't save you.
scenario: At midnight a limited-edition sneaker drop opens. Traffic jumps to 8,000 requests per second, and 40% of them are writes: carts, reservations and orders.

Last time, the team panicked and added two read replicas. It didn't help: every write still lands on the single Postgres primary, which commits about 1,000 writes per second. Checkout timed out for most buyers.
Take every order, keep checkout fast, and make sure nothing piles up unprocessed. Writes can be confirmed and processed a moment later.

objectives.label: Average latency at or below 60 ms
No queue backlog (writes processed as fast as they arrive)

hints: Select the Orders DB after running: SQL replicas are read replicas, so writes are capped at one primary's 1,000 rps. That is the wall you're hitting, and more replicas can't move it.

A Message Queue looks like the answer: it confirms writes instantly. Try putting one in front of Postgres and watch the backlog. A queue only buys time; if its consumer is slower than the arrival rate, orders pile up forever.

You need a store that scales writes. A NoSQL store adds write capacity with each shard (×2 = 10,000 rps). Send writes to it (directly, or through a ×2 queue), add a cache for the 4,800 reads, and keep two of everything for reliability.
explanation: Read replicas scale reads, not writes. With single-primary replication, write throughput is capped by one machine no matter how many replicas you add.

Queues decouple accepting work from doing it, but they don't create capacity. Average consumer throughput must be at least the average arrival rate, or the backlog grows without bound and orders land hours late. That's why queue → Postgres still fails here.

The real fix is a write-scalable store: a partitioned NoSQL table (sharded by order ID or user ID) gains write capacity with every shard. This simulator works on average rates, so the store alone passes. In production you'd still put a queue in front to absorb the first-second burst of a drop, which averages hide.
Real flash sales add more: idempotency keys so retries don't double-charge, inventory reservation with TTLs, a waiting room to admit buyers at a controlled rate, and rate limits per user.
